title: Rabies Demands Quarantine; Pet Theft Demands Abolition
excerpt: Rabies exposure can kill after symptoms begin. Pet theft and uninspected transport expose enforcement gaps. Vietnam needs quarantine, traceability, and abolition by 2030.
body_html:
Rabies leaves no room for delay: once clinical symptoms appear, disease is virtually 100% fatal. That danger does not prove every traded dog carries rabies, and it does not establish that household exposure incidents came from commercial trade. It does establish why sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and illegal transport demand strict control.

WHO guidance states that exposure usually occurs when infected saliva enters through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes. Seek urgent medical assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis, including vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Treatment must begin before symptoms develop.

“Farm-raised” cannot erase a stolen pet

A claim that animals are farm-raised does not verify origin. Proof requires traceable ownership, lawful transport documents, veterinary inspection, quarantine compliance, and records linking animal to source. Without that chain, stolen companion animals and legally sourced animals cannot be reliably distinguished. Pet theft turns family loss into profit. It also destroys public trust in every checkpoint and market claim.

Tradition cannot excuse an enforcement vacuum

Lawful food activity, regulatory breaches, animal theft, poisoning, and illegal transport are different matters. Tradition cannot legalize theft, evade quarantine, or excuse unsafe handling. Community safety requires authorities to identify animals, inspect transport, enforce veterinary controls, investigate theft networks, and publish accountable outcomes.

Vietnamese families and advocates are already demanding stronger protection for people and animals. Official rabies-control targets are not the same as SDE’s campaign demand: complete nationwide abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030.

Turn public concern into a public demand

Sign SDE’s petition calling for nationwide abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition, add your name to a public demand for action, and follow campaign updates as that demand reaches decision-makers.

WHO guidance says exposure usually involves infected saliva entering through bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. After possible exposure, wash the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, then seek urgent medical care for post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms develop.

That health warning does not prove every traded dog carries rabies. It does show why sick animals, uninspected slaughter, illegal transport, and quarantine evasion create unacceptable biosecurity gaps. Household exposure incidents and commercial supply chains must be investigated as separate dimensions of risk.

“Farm-raised” claims cannot erase stolen companions. Without traceable origin, lawful transport documents, veterinary inspection, and quarantine records, buyers cannot know whether animals came from legitimate sources or theft networks. Vietnamese families deserve protection from criminals who turn lost pets and weak enforcement into profit.

Community solidarity can force reform. Demand transparent inspections, real traceability, enforcement against theft and illegal transport, and complete abolition by 2030.
